Genome Size and the Nucleoid vs. Nucleus

blocks.x: The human haploid genome contains roughly 3 picograms (pg) of DNA (about 3.2 billion base pairs) — a figure worth memorizing directly, as it is commonly tested. In prokaryotes, DNA is not enclosed by a nuclear envelope but is condensed into a region called the nucleoid; this is distinct from a nucleosome (a eukaryotic chromatin packaging unit) and from a viroid (an infectious naked-RNA plant pathogen), both of which are common distractors for this term.
Eukaryotic DNA is compacted through several hierarchical levels so that roughly 2 meters of DNA fits into a nucleus a few micrometers across:

items: Nucleosome: the fundamental repeating unit of chromatin — about 147 bp of DNA wrapped roughly 1.65–2 times around a histone octamer core, giving the classic "beads on a string" appearance at 10 nm resolution.
30 nm fiber: the nucleosome "string" is further coiled/zigzagged, with linker histone H1 stabilizing this next level of compaction.
Chromatin loops: the 30 nm fiber is organized into large loops attached to a non-histone protein scaffold/matrix.
Condensed metaphase chromosome: further supercoiling of the loops yields the fully condensed, visibly banded chromosome seen at mitotic metaphase — the most compact state, used for karyotyping.

blocks.x: Histones are small, evolutionarily conserved, positively charged (basic) proteins, rich in the basic amino acids lysine and arginine, which allow them to bind tightly and non-specifically to the negatively charged phosphate backbone of DNA. There are five main histone classes:

c: Form the nucleosome "core" — two copies of each make up the histone octamer around which DNA wraps

H3 and H4 are the most evolutionarily conserved and are particularly rich in arginine; core histones are present in the nucleosome in a fixed 2:2:2:2 stoichiometry (i.e., approximately equimolar to one another, not H1)
"Linker histone" — binds to the DNA between nucleosomes ("linker DNA") and the nucleosome itself, promoting coiling into the 30 nm fiber and higher-order chromatin structure

Richest in lysine; is the most variable histone across species/tissues; it is absent from the core nucleosome particle itself (the nucleosome core lacks H1); most histone synthesis occurs during S phase, coordinated with DNA replication so new nucleosomes can be assembled on newly synthesized DNA

blocks.x: Non-histone chromosomal proteins (the "acidic proteins" of chromatin, including transcription factors, HMG proteins, and scaffold/matrix proteins) contrast with histones in several ways: histones generally suppress/repress gene activity by packaging DNA, whereas non-histone proteins often stimulate gene activity (e.g., transcription factors); non-histone proteins are synthesized throughout the cell cycle (not restricted to S phase like histones); and they show much greater structural variation between species and even between tissues of the same organism, reflecting their regulatory, cell-type-specific roles.
Heterochromatin is subdivided into two types:

items: Constitutive heterochromatin: permanently condensed in all cells and at all times (e.g., centromeric and telomeric regions, satellite DNA), gene-poor, and largely made of repetitive DNA.

Facultative heterochromatin: can be condensed in some cells/at some times but euchromatic in others — the classic example is the inactivated X chromosome in female mammalian cells. Because one X is transcriptionally silenced (X-inactivation, the Lyon hypothesis) to achieve dosage compensation with XY males, a female is functionally hemizygous for most X-linked genes, and the inactive X is composed of facultative heterochromatin (visible cytologically as the Barr body). Correspondingly, the active X chromosome carries more transcriptionally engaged euchromatin than the (largely heterochromatic) Y chromosome.

blocks.x: The Barr body (sex chromatin / "X chromatin") is seen as a drumstick-shaped appendage on neutrophil nuclei or as a chromocenter in interphase nuclei of buccal/oral smear cells; because it represents condensed, inactive chromatin, "euchromatin" is precisely the term that does not apply to it. Sex chromatin frequency is fairly consistent across different tissue sampling sites (oral smear, amniotic/chorionic epithelium) in a given individual, since X-inactivation is a stable, clonally inherited cellular state established early in embryogenesis.

Epigenetic silencing: beyond structural condensation, genes can be actively silenced by methylation of cytosine residues (typically at CpG islands in promoter regions), which recruits repressive chromatin complexes and makes transcription of that DNA segment unlikely — this is mechanistically distinct from histone acetylation (which loosens chromatin and generally activates transcription) and from retrotransposition (mobile element insertion).

A metaphase chromosome consists of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere (primary constriction), which divides each chromatid into a short arm (p, from French "petit") and a long arm (q). Centromere position defines four morphological classes:

c: Very short p arm, often bearing a satellite

blocks.x: Notably, no normal human chromosome is telocentric — all human chromosomes have at least a small p arm, so telocentric chromosomes are found in some other species but not physiologically in humans. The human X chromosome is a (sub)metacentric chromosome, not acrocentric.
The telomere caps each chromosome end and is essential for genome stability. Key facts:

items: Human telomeric DNA is a tandem repeat rich in guanine and cytosine (the repeat sequence is TTAGGG on one strand).

Telomeres are the only region of the chromosome where the very end of the DNA is effectively single-stranded (a 3′ single-stranded G-rich overhang that folds into a protective T-loop), distinguishing them from the centromere or secondary constrictions.

Telomeres progressively shorten with each round of replication (the "end-replication problem") because conventional DNA polymerases cannot fully replicate the lagging strand's 5′ end; the enzyme telomerase can add repeats to counteract this in germline/stem cells but is largely inactive in most somatic cells, contributing to replicative senescence.

Fanconi anemia, a chromosome-instability/DNA-repair disorder, is associated with accelerated telomere shortening (short telomeres), on top of its hallmark chromosomal breakage and interstrand crosslink sensitivity.
Telomeres can be specifically visualized using T-banding, a technique that selectively stains telomeric regions.

blocks.x: A secondary constriction is a non-centromeric narrowing seen on certain chromosomes, often corresponding to the nucleolar organizer region (NOR); on human acrocentric chromosomes this is associated with a satellite — a small chromatin knob distal to the secondary constriction, connected to the rest of the chromosome by a thin stalk. Despite the name, satellite regions of the chromosome contain only DNA/chromatin material without any special RNA hallmark exam distractor issue — importantly, satellite chromosome regions themselves do not carry the centromere (the two are separate landmarks), so a satellite chromosomal appendage is distinguished from "satellite DNA" (a class of repetitive sequence, discussed below) — do not confuse the cytological satellite structure with the molecular satellite-DNA sequence class.
The 22 autosome pairs plus X and Y are traditionally organized into 7 groups (A–G) based on size and centromere position:

c: Large, submetacentric — the longest submetacentric chromosomes
Smallest, acrocentric, with satellites (Y usually without satellites)

blocks.x: Chromosome 1 is the largest human chromosome; chromosome 22 (along with 21) is among the smallest, with chromosome 21 or 22 typically cited as the smallest autosome pair depending on the classification scheme referenced. Karyotype parameters used to characterize and classify each chromosome include its total length, shape, and the centromeric index (ratio of the short arm length to total chromosome length) — all of these together, not any single measure alone.

Regions of relatively frequent, clinically insignificant size variation in constitutive (centromeric) heterochromatin are described classically for chromosomes 1, 9, and 16 — a recognized source of harmless "heteromorphism" in karyotype interpretation, distinguished from true pathogenic variants.
Banding stains reveal a reproducible pattern of light and dark bands along each chromosome, allowing individual chromosome identification and detection of structural rearrangements:

c: The first banding technique described historically; bands fluoresce with varying intensity related to AT/GC content

The most widely used routine banding method; produces dark and light bands. Dark G-bands are heterochromatic, late-replicating, and AT (adenine-thymine)-rich; light G-bands correspond to euchromatin, are early-replicating (not late-replicating — this reversal is a classic "identify the false statement" trap), and are GC (guanine-cytosine)-rich
Produces a band pattern that is the reverse of G-banding — bright/dark bands correspond to GC-rich, early-replicating regions
Selectively stains constitutive heterochromatin, especially at the centromere and other heterochromatic blocks

blocks.x: The International System for Human Cytogenomic Nomenclature (ISCN) describes a karyotype in a compact standard format: total chromosome number, sex chromosome constitution, then any abnormalities.

c: Female with trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) — an extra copy of chromosome 21
Turner syndrome (monosomy X) — in humans, monosomy of the X chromosome is essentially the only monosomy compatible with live birth; autosomal monosomies are generally lethal in utero
Triple-X female — can be an incidental finding, and has been reported in association with conditions such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia in some case series
Female with a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (as in cri-du-chat syndrome) — "del" denotes deletion, with the affected arm and region specified in parentheses

Male carrying a balanced reciprocal translocation ("t") between chromosomes 9 and 22, with breakpoints at the specified bands (the Philadelphia chromosome rearrangement, seen in CML) — the two chromosomes involved and their arm/band breakpoints are listed in matching parentheses

blocks.x: Chromosome bands are numbered outward from the centromere on each arm, using region.band notation, e.g., 1q23 means band 3 of region 2 on the long (q) arm of chromosome 1 — read as chromosome, arm, region, band, in that order (a four-digit-looking notation like "1q23" is really chromosome "1", arm "q", region "2", band "3", not a two-digit band number). A well-known fragile site with clinical significance is Xq27 (associated with Fragile X syndrome), distinguishing it from other, non-pathological fragile sites elsewhere in the genome.

A hydatidiform mole results when a pregnancy arises with only paternal chromosome contributions and no maternal contribution — a complete mole classically has a 46,XX karyotype arising from fertilization of an egg that has lost its own nucleus/maternal chromosomes, followed by duplication of a single sperm's haploid chromosome set (i.e., two haploid sets of paternal chromosomes, with no maternal genetic contribution); it is therefore incorrect to assume complete moles are always 46,XY, since the far more common outcome is 46,XX (a 46,XY mole can occur, from dispermy, but is less typical).

Ploidy refers specifically to the number of complete chromosome sets in a cell (haploid = 1 set, diploid = 2 sets, triploid = 3 sets, etc.) — not simply "number of chromosomes" or "amount of DNA," which can vary independently of ploidy (e.g., in different cell-cycle stages). Euploidy (a normal multiple of the haploid set) and aneuploidy (an abnormal chromosome number, gain/loss of individual chromosomes) both directly affect gene dosage, which underlies the clinical consequences of aneuploidy syndromes.

sections.title: DNA Content Through Gametogenesis and the Cell Cycle

blocks.x: Because DNA replicates in S phase before either meiotic division, a primary spermatocyte (which has completed S phase but not yet undergone meiosis I) contains a tetraploid (4n) amount of DNA, even though it is still diploid in chromosome number — this is the same reasoning by which any diploid somatic cell reaches 4n DNA content by the end of S phase/through G2 (2n in G1, 4n from late S through G2/M, until cytokinesis restores 2n in daughter cells). Following the two meiotic divisions, DNA content drops sequentially — a secondary spermatocyte is 2n, and spermatids/spermatozoa are haploid (1n) — so of the male germ-cell lineage, the primary spermatocyte holds the single highest DNA content, exceeding secondary spermatocytes, spermatids, and mature spermatozoa alike.

items: Satellite DNA: highly repetitive, tandemly arrayed sequences typically found at centromeres and other constitutive heterochromatin blocks; historically named because its distinct buoyant density formed a separate ("satellite") peak on density-gradient centrifugation.

Minisatellite DNA: tandem repeats of intermediate unit length, notably enriched near telomeres, and highly variable in repeat number between individuals (hence "hypervariable" — the basis of classic VNTR/DNA fingerprinting methods).

Microsatellite DNA: very short tandem repeats (1–6 bp units, e.g., dinucleotide CA-repeats) scattered throughout the genome; used in forensic profiling, linkage studies, and are the sequences that undergo characteristic instability in disorders with repeat-expansion mutations.

Alu repeats: short interspersed nuclear elements (SINEs), about 300 bp long, and by far the most abundant repeat family in the human genome (over a million copies, over 10% of genomic DNA) — more abundant than satellite DNA, microsatellites, or rRNA gene repeats.

Transposable elements ("jumping genes"/transposons): mobile DNA sequences that can insert into new genomic locations, and are considered a major driver of genetic variability within a species/population by generating new mutations, insertions, and genomic rearrangements — more so than the comparatively static structural roles of heterochromatin, satellite DNA, or microsatellite DNA.

sections.title: Karyotyping in Practice: Uses and Techniques

blocks.x: A karyotype is the characteristic chromosomal complement (number, size, and shape of chromosomes) of a species or individual, conventionally displayed as an ordered karyogram (an idiogram is a diagrammatic/schematic representation of a karyotype's banding pattern). Karyotyping is used broadly: to detect numerical and structural chromosomal aberrations (aneuploidies, translocations, deletions, duplications, inversions), to study taxonomic/evolutionary relationships between species via chromosome number and banding homology, and indirectly to correlate with certain cellular functions/disease states — in short, karyotyping serves all of these purposes together, which is why species do not share one single "standard" karyotype: each species has its own characteristic chromosome number and morphology.

Mitotic poisons such as colchicine (used deliberately in karyotype preparation to arrest cells at metaphase) act broadly on the mitotic apparatus — interfering with centrioles, the mitotic spindle, and centromere function collectively, since spindle microtubule disruption affects all of these interconnected structures at once.

Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) uses fluorescently labeled DNA probes that hybridize to complementary sequences on chromosomes, allowing rapid, sensitive detection of specific genes, microdeletions, translocations, or aneuploidies directly on chromosome spreads or interphase nuclei — offering much faster turnaround and higher sensitivity than many conventional cytogenetic or diagnostic assays, consistent with the broader principle that nucleic-acid/antibody-probe-based assays generally outperform older conventional diagnostic techniques in speed and sensitivity.

Clinically, disorders like sickle cell anemia arise from a single point mutation in the beta-globin gene and do not alter chromosome number or structure, so they leave the karyotype unaffected — a useful reminder that not all genetic diseases are visible cytogenetically; karyotyping detects only changes large enough to be seen microscopically, while point mutations and small indels require molecular (DNA-level) testing to detect.

Historically, Tjio and Levan were the first to correctly establish that the normal human diploid chromosome number is 46 (revising the previously accepted but incorrect figure of 48), a foundational discovery underpinning all modern human cytogenetics and karyotyping.
